content: The periodic table, in its large version, is a comprehensive representation of the chemical elements. It includes the symbol, atomic number, and standard atomic weight for each element. This table is a systematic arrangement of chemical elements, and its creation is widely attributed to the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869. Mendeleev designed the table to demonstrate recurring, or periodic, trends in the properties of elements. Over time, the structure of the periodic table has been refined and expanded as new elements have been discovered and as theoretical models have advanced to better explain chemical behaviors. The periodic table has become an indispensable tool in the field of chemistry, serving as a framework to classify, organize, and compare the diverse chemical behaviors of elements. Beyond chemistry, it has also found significant applications in physics, biology, engineering, and various industrial fields. As of January 27, 2008, the standard periodic table includes 117 confirmed elements. While element 118 has been synthesized, element 117 had not yet been confirmed at that time. For elements with atomic masses listed in brackets, the value represents the atomic mass of the most stable isotope. If the value is an integer, it corresponds to the mass number of the most stable isotope. In all other cases, the value reflects the relative atomic mass of the element based on its common terrestrial isotopic composition, as defined by the Atomic Weights of the Elements 2001. This value also includes an uncertainty, indicated in parentheses. For instance, the atomic mass of hydrogen is listed as 1.00794(7), meaning that the relative atomic mass of hydrogen in its typical terrestrial isotopic composition is 1.00794 atomic mass units (u), with an uncertainty of 0.00007 u. This variability primarily arises from local differences in isotopic composition across the Earth. For certain elements that have not yet been discovered, their atomic masses are only estimates.
